title: Punishments
bareActText: The punishments to which offenders are liable under the provisions of this Sanhita are— (a) Death; (b) Imprisonment for life; (c) Imprisonment, which is of two descriptions, namely:— (1) Rigorous, that is, with hard labour; (2) Simple; (d) Forfeiture of property; (e) Fine; (f) Community Service.
plainMeaning: This section is the menu of punishments a court can hand down under the BNS: death, imprisonment for life, imprisonment (rigorous or simple), forfeiture of property, fine, and community service. The headline change from the IPC is that community service now appears as a recognised punishment. It can only be imposed where a particular offence provides for it — for example ss.202, 209, 303(2), 355 and 356(2).
ingredients: Punishment must be one of the six kinds listed
Imprisonment is either rigorous (with hard labour) or simple
Community service is newly listed, and is available only where an offence provides for it
punishment: Not applicable — this section defines the kinds of punishment rather than an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds broadly to s.53 IPC; community service is newly added as a listed punishment.

illustrations: A first-time offender steals goods worth less than ₹5,000 and returns them. Under the proviso to s.303(2) the court punishes him with community service instead of prison.
X is sentenced to rigorous imprisonment and must do hard labour in prison. Y, sentenced to simple imprisonment for the same term, need not.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.4 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023).

title: Commutation of sentence
bareActText: The appropriate Government may, without the consent of the offender, commute any punishment under this Sanhita to any other punishment in accordance with section 474 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Explanation.––For the purposes of this section the expression “appropriate Government” means,–– (a) in cases where the sentence is a sentence of death or is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the Union extends, the Central Government; and (b) in cases where the sentence (whether of death or not) is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends, the Government of the State within which the offender is sentenced.
plainMeaning: The appropriate Government can replace a punishment with a different one without the offender's agreement, following the procedure in s.474 of the BNSS. The Explanation decides which Government that is: the Central Government for a death sentence or for an offence under a law on a Union matter, and the State Government where the offender was sentenced for an offence under a law on a State matter.
ingredients: Power lies with the appropriate Government
No consent of the offender is required
Commutation follows the procedure in s.474 BNSS
Central Government: death sentences and offences under laws on Union matters
State Government (where sentenced): offences under laws on State matters
punishment: Not applicable — this section confers a power to commute, not a punishment.

ipcReference.changeNote: Consolidates the IPC's commutation powers and the definition of 'appropriate Government' (s.55A) into one section, and routes commutation through s.474 BNSS.

illustrations: A death sentence is to be commuted. Under the Explanation, the Central Government is the appropriate Government, whatever law the offence was under.
A person sentenced in Maharashtra for an offence under a law on a State matter can have the sentence commuted by the Government of Maharashtra, without being asked for consent.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.5 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023).

title: Fractions of terms of punishment
bareActText: In calculating fractions of terms of punishment, imprisonment for life shall be reckoned as equivalent to imprisonment for twenty years unless otherwise provided.
plainMeaning: When a rule needs a fraction of a sentence to be worked out, imprisonment for life is treated as twenty years for that calculation — unless the law provides otherwise. It is only a calculation rule and does not turn a life sentence into a twenty-year sentence.
ingredients: Applies when calculating a fraction of a term of punishment
Imprisonment for life counts as twenty years for that purpose
Unless otherwise provided
punishment: Not applicable — this is a rule of calculation.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.57 IPC; BNS adds the words 'unless otherwise provided'.

illustrations: A provision allows 'one-half' of a punishment that is imprisonment for life. Under s.6, life counts as 20 years, so the maximum works out to 10 years — unless the law provides otherwise.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.6 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023).

title: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple
bareActText: In every case in which an offender is punishable with imprisonment which may be of either description, it shall be competent to the Court which sentences such offender to direct in the sentence that such imprisonment shall be wholly rigorous, or that such imprisonment shall be wholly simple, or that any part of such imprisonment shall be rigorous and the rest simple.
plainMeaning: Where an offence allows imprisonment 'of either description', the court chooses the mix: all rigorous, all simple, or partly each.
ingredients: The offence must be punishable with imprisonment of either description
The court may direct the imprisonment to be wholly rigorous, wholly simple, or partly each
punishment: Not applicable — this is a sentencing power.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.60 IPC; retained without substantive change.

illustrations: An offence is punishable with imprisonment of either description for up to 2 years. The court may order 6 months' rigorous imprisonment followed by 18 months' simple imprisonment.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.7 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023).

title: Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc.
bareActText: (1) Where no sum is expressed to which a fine may extend, the amount of fine to which the offender is liable is unlimited, but shall not be excessive. (2) In every case of an offence–– (a) punishable with imprisonment as well as fine, in which the offender is sentenced to a fine, whether with or without imprisonment; (b) punishable with imprisonment or fine, or with fine only, in which the offender is sentenced to a fine, it shall be competent to the Court which sentences such offender to direct by the sentence that, in default of payment of the fine, the offender shall suffer imprisonment for a certain term, in which imprisonment shall be in excess of any other imprisonment to which he may have been sentenced or to which he may be liable under a commutation of a sentence. (3) The term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned in default of payment of a fine shall not exceed one-fourth of the term of imprisonment which is the maximum fixed for the offence, if the offence be punishable with imprisonment as well as fine. (4) The imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of a fine or in default of community service may be of any description to which the offender might have been sentenced for the offence. (5) If the offence is punishable with fine or community service, the imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of the fine or in default of community service shall be simple, and the term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned, in default of payment of fine or in default of community service, shall not exceed,— (a) two months when the amount of the fine does not exceed five thousand rupees; (b) four months when the amount of the fine does not exceed ten thousand rupees; and (c) one year in any other case. (6) (a) The imprisonment which is imposed in default of payment of a fine shall terminate whenever that fine is either paid or levied by process of law; (b) If, before the expiration of the term of imprisonment fixed in default of payment, such a proportion of the fine be paid or levied that the term of imprisonment suffered in default of payment is not less than proportional to the part of the fine still unpaid, the imprisonment shall terminate. Illustration. A is sentenced to a fine of one thousand rupees and to four months’ imprisonment in default of payment. Here, if seven hundred and fifty rupees of the fine be paid or levied before the expiration of one month of the imprisonment, A will be discharged as soon as the first month has expired. If seven hundred and fifty rupees be paid or levied at the time of the expiration of the first month, or at any later time while A continues in imprisonment, A will be immediately discharged. If five hundred rupees of the fine be paid or levied before the expiration of two months of the imprisonment, A will be discharged as soon as the two months are completed. If five hundred rupees be paid or levied at the time of the expiration of those two months, or at any later time while A continues in imprisonment, A will be immediately discharged. (7) The fine, or any part thereof which remains unpaid, may be levied at any time within six years after the passing of the sentence, and if, under the sentence, the offender be liable to imprisonment for a longer period than six years, then at any time previous to the expiration of that period; and the death of the offender does not discharge from the liability any property which would, after his death, be legally liable for his debts.
plainMeaning: This section governs fines and what happens if they are not paid. When the law fixes no maximum, the fine is unlimited but must not be excessive. The court may order imprisonment in default of payment, served on top of any other sentence. If the offence carries imprisonment as well as fine, the default term cannot exceed one-fourth of the maximum imprisonment. If the offence is punishable with fine or community service, default imprisonment must be simple and is capped at two months (fine up to ₹5,000), four months (up to ₹10,000) or one year (otherwise). Default imprisonment ends when the fine is paid or levied, part-payment shortens it proportionally, and an unpaid fine can be recovered for six years after sentence — or longer if the prison term is longer — even from the offender's estate after death.
ingredients: No stated maximum: the fine is unlimited but not excessive (s.8(1))
The court may order imprisonment in default, in excess of any other imprisonment (s.8(2))
Offence with imprisonment and fine: default term ≤ one-fourth of the maximum imprisonment (s.8(3))
Default term may be of any description the offence allowed (s.8(4))
Fine or community service offences: simple imprisonment ≤ 2 months (fine ≤ ₹5,000), 4 months (≤ ₹10,000), 1 year otherwise (s.8(5))
Default imprisonment ends on payment or levy; part-payment shortens it (s.8(6))
Unpaid fine can be levied within six years, or longer if the prison term is longer; death does not free the estate (s.8(7))
punishment: Not applicable — this governs fines and default imprisonment rather than defining an offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Consolidates ss.63-70 IPC into a single section on fines and default imprisonment.

illustrations: R is convicted of an offence punishable with imprisonment up to 2 years and fine, and is fined ₹20,000. The default term cannot exceed 6 months — one-fourth of 2 years.
S is convicted of an offence punishable only with fine and is fined ₹4,000. If S does not pay, the default imprisonment must be simple and cannot exceed 2 months.
T dies three years after being fined, with the fine still unpaid. It can still be recovered from property that is legally liable for his debts.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.8 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023).

title: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences
bareActText: (1) Where anything which is an offence is made up of parts, any of which parts is itself an offence, the offender shall not be punished with the punishment of more than one of such his offences, unless it be so expressly provided. (2) Where— (a) anything is an offence falling within two or more separate definitions of any law in force for the time being by which offences are defined or punished; or (b) several acts, of which one or more than one would by itself or themselves constitute an offence, constitute, when combined, a different offence, the offender shall not be punished with a more severe punishment than the Court which tries him could award for any one of such offences. Illustrations. (a) A gives Z fifty strokes with a stick. Here A may have committed the offence of voluntarily causing hurt to Z by the whole beating, and also by each of the blows which make up the whole beating. If A were liable to punishment for every blow, he might be imprisoned for fifty years, one for each blow. But he is liable only to one punishment for the whole beating. (b) But, if, while A is beating Z, Y interferes, and A intentionally strikes Y, here, as the blow given to Y is no part of the act whereby A voluntarily causes hurt to Z, A is liable to one punishment for voluntarily causing hurt to Z, and to another for the blow given to Y.
plainMeaning: If one offence is really made up of parts that are each offences, the offender is punished only once, unless the law expressly says otherwise. And where an act falls within two or more definitions of offences, or several acts combine into a different offence, the court cannot give a punishment more severe than it could for any one of those offences.
ingredients: An offence made up of parts that are themselves offences: punish for only one, unless expressly provided (s.9(1))
An act falling within two or more definitions of offences (s.9(2)(a))
Several acts combining into a different offence (s.9(2)(b))
In either case: no punishment more severe than the court could award for any one offence
punishment: Not applicable — this limits punishment where offences overlap.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.71 IPC, retained with its two sub-sections and illustrations.

illustrations: V slaps W five times in one continuous assault. V is liable to one punishment for the whole assault, not five separate punishments.
During that assault V also deliberately punches a bystander who steps in. The punch is a separate act, so it can be punished separately.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.9 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023).

title: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, the judgment stating that it is doubtful of which
bareActText: In all cases in which judgment is given that a person is guilty of one of several offences specified in the judgment, but that it is doubtful of which of these offences he is guilty, the offender shall be punished for the offence for which the lowest punishment is provided if the same punishment is not provided for all.
plainMeaning: If a court is sure the person committed one of several listed offences but cannot say which, it punishes for the offence carrying the lowest punishment (where the punishments differ).
ingredients: The person is guilty of one of several specified offences
It is doubtful which one
Punishment is for the offence with the lowest punishment, if they differ
punishment: Not applicable — this is a rule for uncertain findings.
illustrations: The evidence proves that D either committed a theft or dishonestly received the stolen goods, but the court cannot say which. If the two offences carry different punishments, D is punished for the one with the lower punishment.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.10 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023).

title: Solitary confinement
bareActText: Whenever any person is convicted of an offence for which under this Sanhita the Court has power to sentence him to rigorous imprisonment, the Court may, by its sentence, order that the offender shall be kept in solitary confinement for any portion or portions of the imprisonment to which he is sentenced, not exceeding three months in the whole, according to the following scale, namely:— (a) a time not exceeding one month if the term of imprisonment shall not exceed six months; (b) a time not exceeding two months if the term of imprisonment shall exceed six months and shall not exceed one year; (c) a time not exceeding three months if the term of imprisonment shall exceed one year.
plainMeaning: Solitary confinement can only be ordered where the offence allows rigorous imprisonment, and only up to a total of three months, spread according to a scale tied to the length of the sentence: up to 1 month (imprisonment ≤ 6 months), up to 2 months (6 months–1 year), and up to 3 months (over 1 year).
ingredients: The offence must carry power to impose rigorous imprisonment
Solitary confinement is limited to three months in total
Scale: ≤1 month if imprisonment ≤6 months; ≤2 months if 6 months–1 year; ≤3 months if over 1 year
punishment: Not applicable — this is a limited sentencing power.
illustrations: E is sentenced to 10 months' rigorous imprisonment. The court may order solitary confinement of at most 2 months in total, because the term is over 6 months but not over 1 year.

G is convicted of an offence that the Sanhita punishes only with simple imprisonment. Solitary confinement cannot be ordered, because the court has no power to impose rigorous imprisonment for that offence.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.11 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023).

title: Limit of solitary confinement
bareActText: In executing a sentence of solitary confinement, such confinement shall in no case exceed fourteen days at a time, with intervals between the periods of solitary confinement of not less duration than such periods; and when the imprisonment awarded shall exceed three months, the solitary confinement shall not exceed seven days in any one month of the whole imprisonment awarded, with intervals between the periods of solitary confinement of not less duration than such periods.
plainMeaning: Even when solitary confinement is ordered, it can never run more than 14 days at a stretch, and must be separated by gaps at least as long. For sentences over three months, it is capped at seven days in any single month.
ingredients: Solitary confinement must not exceed 14 days at a time
Intervals between periods must be at least as long as the periods
For imprisonment over three months, no more than 7 days of solitary confinement in any one month
punishment: Not applicable — this caps how solitary confinement is executed.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.74 IPC; retained without change in language.

illustrations: H has been ordered 2 months of solitary confinement within a 2-year sentence. Because the sentence exceeds three months, it can be served for no more than 7 days in any one month, with a gap at least as long as each spell.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.12 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023).

title: Enhanced punishment for certain offences after previous conviction
bareActText: Whoever, having been convicted by a Court in India, of an offence punishable under Chapter X or Chapter XVII of this Sanhita with imprisonment of either description for a term of three years or upwards, shall be guilty of any offence punishable under either of those Chapters with like imprisonment for the like term, shall be subject for every such subsequent offence to imprisonment for life, or to imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years.
plainMeaning: A person already convicted by an Indian court of an offence under Chapter X (coins, currency-notes, bank-notes and Government stamps) or Chapter XVII (offences against property) carrying three years or more, who then commits another such offence with like punishment, can be sentenced for the later offence to imprisonment for life or up to ten years.
ingredients: A previous conviction by a Court in India
The earlier offence was under Chapter X or Chapter XVII, punishable with three years or more
A later offence under either of those Chapters with like imprisonment for the like term
Enhanced punishment: imprisonment for life, or up to ten years of either description
punishment: Enhanced: imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description up to ten years, for the qualifying repeat offence.

ipcReference.changeNote: Corresponds to s.75 IPC; now refers to BNS Chapters X and XVII and requires the earlier conviction to be by a Court in India.

illustrations: J was convicted of theft under s.303(2), which carries up to 3 years. He is later convicted of another Chapter XVII offence carrying 3 years or more. For the later offence he can face imprisonment for life or up to 10 years.

verification.source: BNS 2023, s.13 — bare Act text verified verbatim against the official Gazette of India (Extraordinary, Part II Sec. 1, Act No. 45 of 2023, 25 Dec 2023).
